title: Platform Systems & Services: Guidance, How-tos, Dashboards, Runbooks, Roadmap Q1 2026
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Overview

This page collects canonical guidance for the Platform Systems & Services team: standard dashboard templates, alerting policy, operational runbooks, a short retrospective from Q4 2025–Q1 2026, and the near-term roadmap. The intent is to provide a single, searchable reference that engineers and on-call responders can follow during day-to-day ops and incidents.

Goals
- Reduce mean time to detect and resolve (MTTD/MTTR) platform incidents.
- Maintain predictable performance and cost for the control plane and core services.
- Provide clear contribution paths for dashboards, alerts, and runbooks.

Scope
This document covers systems owned by the Platform team:
- platform-control-plane (API router, auth, config service)
- platform-runtime (scheduler, autoscaler, batch workers)
- metrics-collector (Prometheus + exporters)
- logging (Loki + log-forwarders)
- observability stack (Grafana, Tempo)
- alert-router (Alertmanager + PagerDuty integration)

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owners: Platform Systems & Services (team Slack: #eng-platform-ops).
- On-call rotation: platform-sre@redwood.example.com (see team wiki for schedule).
- Playbook owner: Ava Martinez (author) — escalate to Priya Patel (Engineering Manager) for policy changes.

Dashboards & Alerts

Principles
- Dashboards are for troubleshooting: focus on latency, errors, saturation, and recent config changes.
- Alerts are for actionable thresholds only (someone must be able to act).
- Prefer short-lived, high-signal alerts over long noisy thresholds. Use anomaly detection only when it's explainable.

Standard dashboard templates (examples)
| Dashboard | Primary Panels | Owner | Refresh |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Control Plane Overview | request rate, 5xx rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, healthy pod count | platform-control-plane | 15s |
| Scheduler Health | queue backlog, scheduling latency, pending pods, autoscaler decisions | platform-runtime | 30s |
| Inference Gateway | token/sec, model-select latency, downstream error % | infra-inference | 15s |

Example Prometheus queries used in dashboards
- Request rate: sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{service="platform-control-plane"}[1m]))
- 5xx rate: sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{service="platform-control-plane",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{service="platform-control-plane"}[5m]))
- p95 latency (histogram): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="platform-control-plane"}[5m])) by (le))

Alerting guidelines and recommended thresholds
- SLO alignment: configure alerts so that paging events indicate imminent or ongoing SLO degradation.
- Pager thresholds (examples):
  - Control plane error-rate: page when 5xx rate > 0.5% sustained over 5m.
  - High latency (p99): page when p99 request latency > 1s for 5m.
  - Pod deficiency: page when ReplicaSet desired != available for > 3m.
  - Disk pressure: page when node_filesystem_avail_bytes < 10% for system partitions.

Alert routing and severity mapping
- Critical (P1): Service unavailable, SLO violation in progress, or data loss. Route to on-call + paging.
- High (P2): Degraded performance that impacts customers (non-urgent regressions). Route to on-call via Slack + email.
- Medium/Low (P3/P4): Informational alerts and capacity warnings -> Ops channel only.

Escalation play (quick summary)
1) Acknowledge in PagerDuty and post a short summary in #incident-ops.
2) Triage: identify affected service, scope (single-customer vs global) and rollback window.
3) Execute runbook for service (see Runbooks section).
4) If not resolved in 30m, escalate to engineering manager and start incident bridge.

Runbooks (canonical examples)
Each runbook is a short, numbered procedure with commands and expected outcomes; keep them <1 page where possible. Below are abridged runbooks — full versions are in the runbooks repo and linked from related_pages.

Runbook: Control Plane High 5xx Rate
1) Confirm event: check dashboard and run queries to validate spike (see Prometheus queries above).
2) Check recent deploys: gitops commit history and platform-control-plane deployment age (kubectl rollout status).
3) Check error logs: kubectl logs -l app=platform-control-plane --tail=200 | grep -i error.
4) If rollout issues found: rollback to previous stable tag (kubectl rollout undo deployment/platform-control-plane --to-revision=<rev>).
5) If CPU/memory saturation: scale replicas per documented scaling policy and investigate OOM or GC issues.
6) After mitigation: annotate incident in the runbook, close alerts, and start post-incident review.

Runbook: Scheduler Backlog (pending pods)
1) Inspect pending pods: kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide.
2) Check node allocatable resources and taints: kubectl describe nodes | egrep "Allocatable|Taints".
3) If insufficient resources in cluster: trigger autoscaler manual scale or increase reserved capacity in Dedicated pools.
4) If scheduling constraints misconfigured: check pod affinity/taints and admission webhook logs.
5) Mitigate by draining a node and recreating or adding nodes to the pool.

Typical incident flow (role checklist)
- First responder: validate and mitigate using runbook.
- Incident commander (after 15–30m): coordinate communications and triage deeper fixes.
- SRE lead: owns rollback/re-architecture decisions and postmortem.

Post-incident retrospective template (use for blameless review)
- Summary: 1–2 sentence summary of what happened and impact.
- Timeline: bullet list with timestamps, detection, mitigation, resolution.
- Root cause: concise statement.
- Corrective actions: 3 concrete items with owners and ETA.
- Follow-up: tests, alerts tuning, and documentation updates.

Retrospective: Q4 2025 -> Q1 2026 highlights
- What went well:
  - Improved dashboard coverage for control plane endpoints; mean detection time reduced by ~25%.
  - Autoscaler adjustments reduced warm-up-related incidents for batch workers.
- Opportunities:
  - Several noisy alerts remained; target: reduce pager volume 40% by Q2 2026.
  - Need a standard template for release-stage load tests prior to production deploys.

Roadmap (next 90 days)
- Q2 2026 priorities:
  - Centralize dashboard templates in a single repo and auto-deploy to Grafana (owner: Observability Working Group).
  - Implement adaptive alert thresholds for error-rate using rolling baselines.
  - Create a self-serve runbook contributor flow and wiki checklist.
  - Expand synthetic checks for critical routes (api/redwood/health and model-serving ping).

How to contribute (process)
1) Create a PR against the platform-observability repo with dashboard JSON or alertmanager config.
2) Include owner, rationale, and test plan in PR description.
3) Reviewer: at least one SRE + one service owner must approve.
4) After merge: CD job deploys dashboard to staging Grafana; validate for 24h before pushing to prod.

Templates and quick references
- Dashboard PR checklist: purpose, panels list, PromQL queries, owner, refresh rate.
- Runbook template: title, scope, step-by-step, rollback plan, verification steps, postmortem link.
- Alert template: name, query, threshold, severity, runbook link, suppression rules.

References and links

- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/platform-runbooks
